title: Measure what matters: KPIs, formulas and who earned the sale

say: Measure what matters: KPIs, formulas, and who really earned the sale.
This is the video for Module 1 of Marketing Analytics and Reporting.
Many reports say: 40 posts, 120,000 impressions, 2,300 likes. All true. But the owner still cannot answer her real question. Should I keep spending this money, and where?
A strong report starts at the top. The decision, then the business outcome, such as sales or leads.
Below that, channel numbers that explain the result. Activity comes last, only as context. So before you open any dashboard, ask what decision the report must support.
Amaka wants to know whether to raise ad spend in April, and on which platform. Her order sheet shows 95 orders worth 1,710,000 naira in March.

say: That is 450,000 naira in total. Divide revenue by spend, and every 1 naira of marketing was matched by 3.80 naira of sales. Each order cost about 4,737 naira in marketing.
But is 3.8 good? Only the margin can tell. If product, packaging and delivery take 60% of the price, only 40% is left for marketing and overheads. Always ask for the margin first.

say: A measurement plan fixes what you will measure before results arrive, so nobody changes the meaning of success afterwards. Start with the objective, then one primary KPI, a key performance indicator.

panel.heading: A one-page measurement plan
items: Baselines and targets with a date
Two or three segments to compare

say: Add the driver metrics that move it, today's baseline and a target, and the segments you will compare, such as new versus returning customers.

say: ROAS, return on ad spend, uses the revenue one platform says it caused. Each platform reports its own.

panel.heading: ROAS or MER?
left: Revenue credited to ads / ad spend

say: MER, the marketing efficiency ratio, uses real total revenue and total spend. Two platforms cannot inflate it by claiming the same sale. You will use both.

panel.heading: ROAS or MER?
left: Revenue credited to ads / ad spend

say: For example, Halima sells fabrics online from Kano. Last month, 12,000 sessions at 1.2% conversion gave 144 orders. At 20,000 naira each, that is 2,880,000 naira.
She wants 3,000,000 naira. That needs 150 orders, just 6 more.
She can get 500 more sessions, or lift conversion to 1.25%. Showing delivery fees and adding a WhatsApp help button may cost less than ads, so she tests that lever first.
This is the KPI tree. Each branch shows you a lever to pull.

panel.heading: Halima's KPI tree
panel.rule: Revenue = sessions x conversion rate x average order value

say: For example, Bola saw an Instagram ad, later searched on Google, then bought after an email. Attribution is the rule that shares the credit.
Under last click, email looks like the hero.

The first touch gets all the credit. The Instagram ad gets 60,000 naira.
Every touch shares equally: 20,000 naira each to Instagram, Google and email.

say: Meta and Google each count conversions by their own rules, so their totals often add up to more orders than you received.
Attribution also cannot prove cause. In this test, the group that saw retargeting ads made 300 purchases.
A similar group with no ads still made 250. Only the 50 extra were caused by the ads.
So the true cost per extra purchase was 5,000 naira, not the 833 naira the platform reported. That is six times higher.
To remember. Lead with outcomes. Know the margin before you call a result good. Fix your plan and formulas first.
Label every number with its source and rule, and show bad news as clearly as good news.
